name: Acmer P1 10W
tagline: Budget Acmer open-frame: large bed for the price
tldr: Acmer P1 10W is an affordable 400 mm-class open-frame engraver for learning and light gifts. Build and support are budget-tier: great value if you accept DIY tuning.
mainObjective: High-quality hobby and light-business engraving with light, slow cutting

engraveExample.description: Filled photo or logo on birch plywood

cutExample.description: Simple square cut-out from 3 mm basswood

pros: Acmer's own 10W preset engraves wood at 4,800 mm/min (55% power): photos, logos and leather do not need more power
Finest spot of the P1 line (~0.07 mm), which keeps small text and photo dots crisp
Cheapest way into the 400 × 400 mm P1 frame: $259–329, about $70 below the higher-watt P1
cons: Cutting is slow: Acmer's 10W sheet lists 6 mm board at only 150 mm/min, and 3 mm basswood takes ~9–15 min for a 10 × 10 cm square in our benchmark
Black acrylic stops being practical past ~4 mm (70 mm/min on Acmer's settings)
New units are scarce: in October 2026 Acmer's store listed the P1 10W as refurbished only ($229)
beginnerNotes: This profile is the 10W SKU on Acmer P1. Read the TL;DR and benchmarks above, then compare other power options via the chips before buying.
proTips: Run material test grids at engraving speeds first. Add air assist for light cuts. If cut jobs exceed ~30% of your week, open the higher-watt profile on this site and compare times.

editorialDepth.advantages: Acmer P1 10W suits makers who sell marks, photos, and gifts more than daily panel cutting. Reasonable open-frame entry price.
editorialDepth.limitations: Skip if you already quote 4 mm+ cutting in production: see 20W in the line. Not for cast acrylic or bare metal without spray.

faq.question: How thick can the Acmer P1 10W cut?
faq.answer: Acmer's 10W parameter sheet lists 2 mm board at 360 mm/min, 6 mm at 150 mm/min and 7.5 mm at 120 mm/min, all at full power, plus black acrylic at 150 mm/min (2 mm) and 70 mm/min (4 mm). The sheet does not state pass counts. In practice, treat 3–4 mm basswood as comfortable and anything above 6 mm as a slow, multi-pass job with air assist.

faq.question: Is the P1 10W fast enough for photo engraving?
faq.answer: For gifts and small batches, yes. Our benchmark puts a 10 × 10 cm filled photo on birch plywood at ~18–28 min, against ~12–18 min on the P1 20W. Acmer's wood preset for this module is 4,800 mm/min at 55% power, so you are rarely limited by the laser on engraving work.

faq.question: P1 10W or P1 20W: which one should I buy?
faq.answer: Take the 10W if you mainly engrave (photos, leather, slate, signs) and only cut card or 2–3 mm wood now and then: it costs about $70 less ($259–329 vs $329–399). Take the 20W if cut pieces are part of what you sell. Acmer also sells the 20W module on its own ($309 in October 2026), but upgrading later costs more than buying the 20W upfront.

standoutFeatures.title: Fine spot for detail work
standoutFeatures.body: ~0.07 mm spot on the 10W module (vs ~0.08 mm on the 20W): small lettering and photo dithering stay sharp on leather and hardwood.

standoutFeatures.title: Lowest entry price on the P1 frame
standoutFeatures.body: $259–329 for the same 400 × 400 mm frame as the 20W, about $70 less. A refurbished unit was $229 on Acmer's store in October 2026.

standoutFeatures.title: Room to upgrade later
standoutFeatures.body: Acmer sells a 20W module for the P1 ($309 in October 2026), so the frame can stay if cutting becomes the main job.
